transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
- Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Ryland Barton.
A sell-off of AI stocks today dragged the S&P 500
down 3.7%, capping off its worst weekly loss
in more than a year and a half.
The NASDAQ fell more than five and a quarter percent,
meaning it lost all of the gains it's made this year.
NPR's John Ruich has more on how investors
are thinking about the AI industry.
- Many investors have been flip-flopping for months now
between exuberance about the promise of AI
and worries that we're in a bubble.
This week extended a downward slide
that actually started in early October.
AI companies have been pouring billions of dollars
into chips, data centers, and top talent,
but it's not clear that it's all gonna pay off
in profits for them.
- NPR's John Ruich reporting.
President Trump says he and Chinese President Xi
have agreed to what he calls "joint guardrails"
amid the race to develop AI.
NPR's Deepa Shivram reports
it's a notable acknowledgement about the risks involved
with the technology.
- Trump briefed the press on this week's trip to China.
Talk of, quote, "guardrails" is a new move for Trump,
who's always been adamant that the technology
should not have any regulations
because it would hold the U.S. back
in the race against China on AI.
Now he says sometimes the technology can be too powerful.
Neither country has released any further information
on what those joint safeguards could look like
or how they would be implemented.
Trump also said he would continue to push
for the construction of data centers in the U.S.
and will penalize companies
that build them outside the U.S.
Deepa Shivram, NPR News, Washington.
- House Speaker Mike Johnson is pleading
with Republicans to show up to work
during the final month of the party's control of Congress.
Leaders had to cut this past work week short
because not enough members were in Washington
to pass party-line legislation.
In a letter, Johnson said, quote,
"We need every House Republican to remain fully engaged
so we can get even more of our important priorities
signed into law."
In Los Angeles, the man accused
of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades fire
has been found guilty by a federal jury,
Steve Futterman reports.
- The jury reached its verdict
on the third day of deliberations,
finding Jonathan Rinderknecht guilty on both counts.
He was accused of setting the Lachman fire
on January 1st last year, just past midnight.
That fire smoldered underground for a week
and then reemerged as the deadly Palisades fire.
As the verdict was read,
Rinderknecht showed little, if any, emotion.
This was the second time he faced these charges.
In the first trial, the jury was hung 10 to 2 for acquittal.
He now awaits sentencing.
That will come next year.
He faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison
for each of the two counts.
For NPR News, I'm Steve Futterman
at the Federal Courthouse in Los Angeles.
- Third-party vendors at JPMorgan Chase
experienced a cyber attack
that leaked personal information
of thousands of Chase customers
The bank says the leak yesterday is unrelated
to an outage earlier in the week.
The leaked data includes mostly email addresses
and some phone numbers, but not credit card information.
This is NPR News.
Bayer will pay up to seven and a quarter billion dollars
over two decades to settle thousands of US claims
related to its weed killer Roundup.
A Missouri judge approved the settlement,
which covers users diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
Participants could receive between $10,000
and $165,000 depending on their circumstances.
Bayer denies that Roundup causes cancer
when used as directed,
but has sought financial certainty
amid mounting litigation costs.
The Iraqi government has reached a deal
with a major Iran-backed militia
over control of bases near Baghdad.
As NPR's Jana Raff reports,
the move diffuses fears over clashes
between militia fighters and Iraqi security forces.
- Iraqi security officials announced Friday
that government forces would deploy to Jafar Nasser,
where Iran-backed Kataab Hezbollah has bases.
The government has accused the paramilitary group
and some government officials of oil smuggling operations
in the area south of Baghdad.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Azadi
has pledged to disarm Iraq's extensive network
of armed groups that aren't fully under government control.
While some have agreed, Kataab Hezbollah,
one of the most powerful,
has refused to give up its weapons.
Jana Raff, NPR News, Amman.
- The ancient Ulpia Library in Rome has been restored
and is reopening to the public this week.
Located in Emperor Trajan's Forum,
it was initially discovered in the 1930s,
but remained buried for decades.
The library consisted of two buildings
that stored thousands of scrolls.
Archaeologists identified it as the Western Building,
which held Greek language scrolls.
This is NPR News from Washington.

topics.text: AI stock sell-off drives S&P 500 down 3.7% and NASDAQ down over 5%, worst week in over a year
Investors remain torn between AI enthusiasm and bubble fears as AI companies spend billions
Trump says he and Xi agreed to joint AI guardrails, a notable shift on tech regulation
House Speaker Mike Johnson urges Republicans to show up to Washington during final month of control
Jury convicts Jonathan Rinderknecht of setting the 2025 Lachman fire that became the Palisades fire
JPMorgan Chase third-party vendors suffer cyber attack leaking customer email addresses and phone numbers
Bayer agrees to pay up to $7.25 billion over two decades to settle Roundup cancer claims
Iraqi government reaches deal with Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah over bases near Baghdad
Ancient Ulpia Library in Rome's Trajan's Forum restored and reopening to the public
